summary: Describes TESS, an identity-based system for authenticated key exchange, creating signatures, and distributing public keys, built on exponential (discrete-logarithm) methods. It is an informational document.

eli5.summary: A way for two people to make a shared secret and prove who they are, using their names as part of the key.

subtitle: An identity-based cryptographic system for authenticated key exchange using discrete exponentiation

tldr.problem: Secure communication requires both parties to prove their identity and establish shared secret keys, but traditional systems require managing separate public-key infrastructure or central authorities.
tldr.mechanism: TESS uses identity descriptors (like a user's name or email) as part of the cryptographic key material, combined with discrete exponentiation mathematics and self-certified keys generated by a Secure Key Issuing Authority (SKIA).
tldr.outcome: Two parties can authenticate each other and exchange keys without a central authority or third party, using only knowledge of their local SKIA's public parameters.

today: RFC 1824 is an Informational document and has never been on the Internet Standards track. It remains a reference for identity-based cryptography systems using discrete exponentation, though the field has evolved significantly with modern identity-based encryption (IBE) schemes and other approaches.

sections.title: What TESS Is
sections.content:
TESS (The Exponential Security System) is a toolbox of cryptographic mechanisms built on discrete exponentiation — a mathematical operation where computing forward is easy but computing backward (the discrete logarithm problem) is hard. The RFC describes how to use this mathematics for authenticated key exchange, digital signatures, and secure key distribution.

The key insight of TESS is identity-based cryptography: instead of maintaining a separate random public key, a user's identity descriptor (name, email address, or domain name) becomes part of the cryptographic material itself. A trusted local authority, called a SKIA (Secure Key Issuing Authority), creates a user's key pair from this identity descriptor.
sections.eli5: TESS is a system where who you are mathematically becomes how you prove it. A trusted office (the SKIA) takes your name and turns it into your security key.

sections.title: Setup: Keys and Authorities
sections.content:
The TESS system has two levels of keys. First, every SKIA generates its own key pair from a large prime p, a primitive root generator g, and a secret exponent x, publishing (p, g, y) where y = g^x mod p. Second, each user's SKIA generates a user's key pair by creating an ElGamal signature on the user's Identity Descriptor—a structured description of who they are, including name, organization, expiry date, and key management details.

The user's public key is the pair (Id[A], r[A]) (identity descriptor plus a signature component), and the secret is s[A]. Critically, k[A], the random value used during key generation, must be destroyed immediately after use, because knowing both s[A] and k[A] would allow a user to compute the SKIA's secret x.
sections.eli5: A SKIA picks three secret numbers and publishes information based on them. When you sign up, the SKIA uses your name and a random number to create your public and secret keys, then destroys the random number so it cannot be reused.

sections.title: Authentication Methods
sections.content:
TESS offers three kinds of authentication. Zero Knowledge Authentication lets a user prove their identity to someone without needing a session key afterward—useful for one-time authentication. Unilateral Authentication lets one party (Bob) send a message encrypted with a shared key that only the recipient (Alice) can decrypt, without Bob authenticating himself. Mutual Authentication extends this so both parties exchange challenges and responses to cryptographically verify they each control their secret key, establishing shared session keys for both directions.

All methods rely on the self-certification property: Bob can compute a verification value Y[A] from Alice's public key and the SKIA's public information alone, without trusting any third party. This Y[A] ties Alice's secret key to her identity descriptor mathematically.
sections.eli5: You can prove who you are in three ways: without needing a secret (just prove you know it), one-way (so others can send you secret messages), or both-ways (so you both know you're talking to the right person).

sections.title: Digital Signatures and Non-Escrowed Keys
sections.content:
Message signing in TESS works by generating an ElGamal signature on a hash of the message. The procedure is nearly identical to key generation: the author generates a random K, computes R and S values, and the signed message becomes (m, Id[A], r[A], R, S). A receiver verifies the signature by checking an equation involving the sender's public values and the message hash.

A security concern: because the SKIA knows the user's secret key s[A] during normal key generation, the SKIA could forge signatures or decrypt messages. To prevent this, TESS offers non-escrowed key generation, where the user creates a random value a and gives g^a to the SKIA. The SKIA then creates a modified key from which the user derives the actual secret by multiplying by a^-1. Now the SKIA never learns the true s[A].
sections.eli5: Signing a message uses the same math as making your key. Normally the office knows your secret key and could forge your signature, but a special trick lets the office make your key without ever learning your actual secret.

sections.title: Multiple Authorities and Hierarchies
sections.content:
TESS works with a single SKIA, but scales to multiple authorities through hierarchical trust. In a hierarchy, a User at level n becomes a SKIA at the same level, issuing keys to Users at level n+1. The root SKIA has level 0. Because a User's secret key is identical to the SKIA authority key that the same entity would use, the scheme unifies users and issuers mathematically.

Two users with keys from different SKIAs can still authenticate by building a chain of trust: Bob learns Alice's root SKIA's parameters reliably, then verifies each SKIA in the chain from root to Alice by iteratively computing Y values using the verification equations. This forms a certification path where each step is a nested signature. The RFC gives a practical example: a DNS-based hierarchy where every domain is a SKIA, so a user danisch@ira.uka.de has their key signed by ira.uka.de, which was signed by uka.de, which was signed by the root domain de.
sections.eli5: One office can authorize smaller local offices to issue their own keys, forming a chain of trust. Anyone who trusts the top office can follow the chain to trust anyone below it, using only math—no central directory needed.
